blocks.text: Image of the week

blocks.alt: Microscopic image of a ballpoint pen tip, showing swirling metallic silver and purple patterns
blocks.caption: Photograph: Justin Theodore Benttinen/Nikon Small World

blocks.text: Sheep dung, snails and mouse brains are all beautiful … if you look closely enough. This artwork could be a newly discovered planet or an abstract piece by Stanley Donwood for Radiohead’s A Moon Shaped Pool, but the truth is tinier: this is the tip of a ballpoint pen, a winning entry from the Nikon Small World photography competition .

blocks.text: Masterpiece of the week
St Jerome and the Lion: Predella Panel by Fra Filippo Lippi and Workshop, 1455-60

blocks.alt: Saint Jerome kneels beside a lion, gently holding its paw, in a rocky landscape
blocks.caption: Photograph: piemags/Alamy

blocks.text: Filippo Lippi was the wild man of early 15th-century Florentine art, if the stories told about him in the Renaissance are anything to go by. It was even said his patron Cosimo de’ Medici had to lock him in the Medici palace to stop his debauchery. There is a core of fact behind the tales, as Filippo – a friar – is known from legal records to have had children with an escaped nun, Lucrezia Buti. Their son Filippino also became an artist. But whatever his life was like, there’s no lack of piety in this painting of the early Christian Jerome, a real historical figure who translated the Bible into Latin. The lion tamely lets the holy man pull a thorn from its paw, in an intricately painted mountainous landscape with a pink church. Jerome concentrates on his work, as you would if you were de-thorning a dangerous big cat. This is just a small panel from the base of an altarpiece but it packs in the emotion and humanity that makes Lippi a great artist, in spite of, or because of, his sins.
National Gallery, London
